strengths: Introduces a valuable large-scale behavioral benchmark: a classical two-dot same/different object judgment paradigm scaled to 1020 trials over 255 naturalistic COCO images with 72 participants, careful experimental controls (distance matching between conditions, counterbalancing, eye-tracking exclusion of fixation breaks), which fills a genuine gap between low-level Gestalt/contour studies and naturalistic object perception.

Comprehensive and well-motivated model comparison across architectures (ViT vs ConvNext) and training objectives (DINO, MAE, supervised, distilled), with matched-capacity comparisons that allow the important disentangling of training objective vs. architecture (e.g., supervised ViT-B vs. DINO ViT-B; supervised vs. distilled ConvNext-B).

The proposed object-centricity metric (ROC analysis of patch affinity maps against ground-truth object boundaries) is simple, supervision-light, interpretable, and shown to correlate strongly with behavioral alignment across all models, providing a plausible representational account of why self-supervised models align better with human grouping.

The Gram-matrix distillation experiment is the most mechanistically interesting part: it moves beyond correlational evidence by showing that actively shaping pairwise patch-similarity structure in supervised models improves both object-centricity and behavioral alignment, converging with independent evidence from DINOv3's design.

The paper is clearly written, the behavioral methodology is rigorous (noise-ceiling normalization for RT prediction, cross-validation, multiple seeds), and the qualitative behavioral signatures (same-object advantage, distance-by-object interaction) are reproduced by the best model.
weaknesses: The Gram-alignment experiment lacks critical controls. The observed gains could partly stem from any feature distillation or from additional ImageNet fine-tuning, rather than Gram structure per se. Controls such as (a) fine-tuning without any distillation loss, (b) distilling raw features or attention maps instead of the Gram matrix, and (c) Gram anchoring to a supervised teacher are needed to support the causal claim that 'Gram matrix structure is an active contributor' to behavioral alignment.

Statistical rigor is insufficient in key analyses. The central claim that object-centricity AUC predicts behavioral alignment rests on a correlation across only ~9 models with no reported significance test, confidence intervals, or error bars (e.g., in Fig. 4A and Fig. 6B). Differences between adjacent models (e.g., DINOv2 vs. DINOv3) are not tested.

The grouping-accuracy readout is trained on ~30k synthetic trials with COCO ground-truth annotations, so it measures agreement with annotation-derived ground truth rather than human judgments; the relationship between this accuracy and the human behavioral data could be discussed and analyzed more explicitly, including potential confounds (e.g., object-category familiarity of different models).

The model space is limited: only ViT-Base variants, one patch size, and a small number of training recipes. Claims that 'training objective matters more than architecture' would be strengthened by more architectures, scales, and patch sizes, and by additional self-supervised objectives beyond DINO and MAE.

Reproducibility is not addressed: there is no statement about releasing the behavioral dataset, dot-placement algorithm, readout training code, or Gram-alignment training details (hyperparameters, loss weights, number of steps are not specified), which is problematic given the benchmark is a primary contribution.

The contribution is partly confirmatory: that DINO-style models have object-centric patch features is well established (LOST, TokenCut, dense descriptor work, all cited), so the novelty rests mainly on the behavioral benchmark and the Gram-alignment intervention; the paper would benefit from a more explicit positioning of what is new relative to that literature.

Potential circularity in the object-centricity evaluation: ground-truth object masks come from COCO, whose annotation conventions (what counts as one object) may interact with the training distribution of the evaluated models; this is discussed only implicitly.

strengths: The paper introduces a valuable large-scale behavioral benchmark: a two-dot same/different object judgment task on naturalistic COCO scenes, scaling a classical psychophysics paradigm (~1020 trials, 72 subjects) with careful experimental controls (distance-matched conditions, counterbalancing, eye-tracking, fixation-break exclusion). The replication of the same-object advantage and distance interaction validates the paradigm.

The model evaluation is reasonably broad, covering Transformer and convolutional architectures across supervised, self-supervised (DINO family, MAE), and distilled training regimes, and the noise-normalized Spearman correlation procedure against a human split-half ceiling is methodologically sound and well described.
The object-centricity metric based on ROC analysis of patch affinity maps is simple, supervision-free, and interpretable; the layer-wise and head-wise analyses add useful descriptive depth.

The Gram-alignment experiment is the most interesting contribution, as it moves from correlational (AUC predicts behavioral alignment across 9 models) to interventional evidence, and converges with independent evidence from the DINOv3 design that Gram anchoring improves dense feature quality.

The paper is clearly written, well organized, and honest about remaining gaps (e.g., the distance between best model and human noise ceiling; that perfect object-centricity is not necessarily desirable).
weaknesses: The Gram-alignment experiment lacks a critical control condition: the supervised models are simultaneously fine-tuned on ImageNet classification, so the reported gains (8-18 points) could partly or wholly reflect additional fine-tuning rather than Gram distillation per se. Controls such as fine-tuning without the Gram loss, or distilling Gram matrices from a weaker/non-object-centric model, are needed to support the causal claim that 'Gram matrix structure is not merely a byproduct but an active contributor.'

The central correlational claim (object-centricity predicts behavioral alignment) rests on only ~9 models in Fig. 6B, with no statistical significance testing, and with training objective confounded with data scale (e.g., DINOv2/v3 vs. DINO/MAE differ in more than the objective). The 'training objective matters more than architecture' conclusion, while plausible given matched-architecture comparisons, would benefit from more models or statistical treatment.

The RT prediction setup has potential confounds: the MLP readout for grouping is trained on ~30,000 synthetic trials derived from COCO annotations, so model performance partly measures agreement with annotation quality/noise rather than human perception; and only the last layer is used for most comparisons despite the paper's own analysis showing object-centricity varies substantially across layers, raising a question of whether a fairer multi-layer comparison would change model rankings.

The behavioral dataset is modest in size (255 experimental images, one condition per image per subject), and mean RT per trial is estimated across subsets of subjects, limiting the precision of the trial-level RT targets that models are asked to predict.

Key experimental details needed for reproducibility are missing or underspecified: MLP readout hyperparameters and training details for RT regression, Gram-distillation loss formulation and weighting, fine-tuning schedules, and no explicit statement about code/data release for the benchmark.

The manuscript does not include a limitations or societal-impact discussion beyond brief mentions embedded in the conclusion, and the behavioral results section is largely confirmatory of known effects, so the novel empirical payload is concentrated in the RT-prediction and Gram-alignment results, which carry the weaknesses noted above.

strengths: The paper introduces a valuable new behavioral benchmark: a large-scale (72 subjects, ~1020 analyzed trials) same/different object judgment paradigm on naturalistic COCO scenes, substantially scaling up classical two-dot grouping experiments that previously used only ~24 hand-selected images. This addresses a real gap, since most grouping work has focused on synthetic Gestalt stimuli.

The experimental methodology is careful and rigorous: eye-tracking with fixation exclusion, distance-matched dot placement between same/different conditions to preclude low-level distance confounds, counterbalancing across participants, and noise-ceiling normalization for RT prediction (split-half reliability with 20 subject splits) are all appropriate and well-executed psychophysical practices.

The model evaluation is reasonably broad and well-controlled (Transformer vs. ConvNext, DINO/DINOv2/DINOv3/MAE vs. supervised, with/without large-scale pretraining, plus a distilled convolutional model), enabling a clean dissociation of training objective from architecture. The conclusion that objective matters more than architecture is well supported by same-architecture comparisons.

The object-centricity metric (ROC over thresholded affinity maps against ground-truth object boundaries, requiring no object-level supervision) is simple, interpretable, and the layer-wise and head-wise analyses (Fig. 5) add mechanistic texture. The correlation between object-centric AUC and behavioral alignment across models (Fig. 6B) provides a unifying explanatory account.

The Gram-alignment intervention (Section 4.3) elevates the paper from correlational to (partially) causal: fine-tuning supervised models with Gram distillation from DINOv3 improves grouping accuracy, object-centric AUC, and behavioral alignment, and converges with independent evidence from the DINOv3 report that Gram anchoring drives dense feature quality. This is the most interesting scientific contribution.

The paper is clearly written, with a logical progression from behavior to modeling to mechanism, and honest discussion of limitations (gap to noise ceiling, tension between perfect object-centricity and feature sensitivity).
weaknesses: Statistical support for key claims is thin. Fig. 4A (behavioral alignment per model) and Fig. 6B report no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite 10 seeds and 20 splits being available; the object-centricity-vs-alignment relationship in Fig. 6B rests on only 9 model points, so claims that object-centricity is 'a general principle' are under-powered.

The MLP readout is trained on ~30,000 synthetically generated COCO trials using each model's own features. Differences in grouping accuracy across models could partly reflect how well a 2-layer MLP can linearly decode features in general, rather than object-centric structure per se; a control using an alternative readout or probing procedure would strengthen the comparison.

The RT-prediction analysis uses only 1,020 trials with 10-fold cross-validation on what appear to be relatively similar COCO images; with trial-level features concatenated from just two patches, mild overfitting and image-content leakage across folds cannot be fully ruled out. Reporting per-fold variance and subject-level generalization would help.

Novelty of the object-centric metric is modest: evaluating token-affinity maps against ground-truth segmentation masks via ROC-type analysis is closely related to existing evaluations of DINO attention/features (LOST, TokenCut, dense descriptor work). The framing as a 'novel metric' overstates the contribution somewhat.

Gram-alignment fine-tuning (Section 4.3) lacks methodological detail in the manuscript: the distillation loss form, layer(s) at which Gram matching is applied, loss weighting, training schedule, and whether ImageNet classification accuracy is preserved are not reported, hindering reproducibility. The paper also does not explicitly state whether the behavioral benchmark and code will be released, which matters for a benchmark-type contribution.

Scale of models evaluated is limited to Base-size variants; given claims about model generations and scaling, testing whether alignment improves with model size would materially strengthen the 'steady improvement across model generations' narrative.

No explicit limitations or ethics/societal-impact statement is included (the limitations discussion is embedded in the conclusion); for a human-subjects study, a brief statement on data handling and participant consent scope would be appropriate.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely new, large-scale behavioral benchmark: the classical two-dot same/different object paradigm scaled to 255 naturalistic COCO images (~1020 trials, 72 subjects) with careful experimental controls (fixation enforcement via eye tracking, distance-matched conditions, counterbalancing, practice trials, RT/accuracy/d-prime/criterion analyses in supplementary).

Model comparison is methodologically careful: noise-ceiling normalization for RT prediction, nested cross-validation with multiple seeds, a linear-readout control confirming the ranking is not an artifact of MLP capacity, and condition-split correlations showing alignment is not driven by one condition or outliers.

The proposed object-centricity metric (ROC over patch affinity maps against ground-truth masks) is simple, supervision-free at the object level for the models, and its correlation with behavioral alignment (r=0.95) provides a substantive representational account of what drives human-like grouping.

The Gram-matrix distillation intervention is the most convincing causal element: it includes appropriate controls (CLS-token distillation baseline isolating patch correlation structure as the active ingredient, unchanged ImageNet top-1 accuracy), and it converges with the independent DINOv3 Gram-anchoring finding, strengthening the mechanistic claim.

Conclusions are appropriately hedged (e.g., acknowledging architecture/objective confounds, the remaining gap to the human noise ceiling, and that perfect object-centricity is not the goal). Code and data availability is stated.

The work is well positioned relative to related literature (LOST/TokenCut, dense ViT descriptors, visual anagrams, contour-integration studies) and extends the question from low-level Gestalt cues to naturalistic object grouping.
weaknesses: The key cross-model correlation between object-centricity and behavioral alignment rests on only 9 models, and the model set is confounded (dataset scale, training regime, and architecture co-vary); the authors acknowledge this, but the strength of the 'object-centricity is the general linking principle' claim is limited by the small, non-orthogonal sample.

Behavioral coverage is modest: 255 images from a single dataset (COCO) with a single subject population and a single lab; the benchmark's generality and cross-dataset robustness are untested. Ground truth is COCO annotation masks, which are category-level and imperfect for part-level grouping judgments.

Even the best model achieves raw r≈0.35 (normalized 0.83) against a noise ceiling of 0.42, i.e., a substantial fraction of behavioral variance is unexplained; claims of 'human-like' grouping should be tempered accordingly (partly acknowledged).

Potential confounds in the readout are not fully ruled out: the grouping readout is trained on 30k synthetic trials generated with the same COCO-annotation-based dot-placement algorithm, so models may partly learn annotation-style segmentation or low-level cues (dot distance, local contrast) rather than human grouping per se; a low-level-feature baseline readout would help disentangle this.

The Gram-alignment experiment fine-tunes only the last block and distills from a single teacher (DINOv3 ViT B); generality of the Gram-anchoring conclusion across teachers, block choices, and loss weightings is not explored, and the mechanistic link to DINOv3's own training remains inferential rather than demonstrated.

Reproducibility is weakened by a placeholder 'Code and data are available here' link; several details (dot-placement algorithm specifics, Gram distillation hyperparameters beyond those given) rely on promised code.

Some evidence is presented only in supplementary material with limited statistical detail in the main text (e.g., significance tests for model ranking differences), making it hard to judge whether, e.g., DINOv3 vs DINOv2 or MAE differences are meaningful.

strengths: The behavioral experiment is well executed: eye-tracked fixation control, counterbalanced conditions, matched dot distances, careful exclusion criteria, and thorough supplementary analyses of accuracy, d-prime, criterion, and RT distributions lend credibility to the benchmark.
Scaling the classical two-dot paradigm to 255 naturalistic COCO scenes (1,020 trials) is a meaningful and useful contribution to the community, and the data are stated to be released along with code.
The model comparison is sensibly controlled in places: supervised vs. self-supervised models share the same ViT-Base architecture, and a noise-ceiling normalization procedure is properly described.

The Gram-distillation experiment includes a valuable control (CLS-token distillation baseline showing no improvement while Gram distillation does), which strengthens the mechanistic claim that patch-level correlation structure is the active ingredient; a linear-readout baseline similarly guards against MLP-capacity artifacts.

The finding that DINOv3 ConvNext performs well supports the claim that the training objective, not architecture alone, drives object-centric representations, and the connection to Gram anchoring in DINOv3 is a coherent narrative.
weaknesses: The behavioral benchmark is small and narrow: 255 images from a single dataset, a single lab population, and only 1,020 trials. The raw Spearman correlations are modest (best model r=0.35) and the noise ceiling itself is only 0.42, meaning even the best model explains a small fraction of trial-level behavioral variance; the paper's claims of 'strong' behavioral alignment should be tempered accordingly.

Critically, there is no low-level control baseline. Reaction times could plausibly be predicted from simple cues (local texture similarity, contrast, distance, boundary salience) without any object-level grouping. Without pixel-level, texture-similarity, or distance-only baselines, the claim that the models capture 'object grouping' per se—rather than generic low-level similarity—is not established. This is the most consequential missing experiment.

There is a circularity concern in the object-centricity metric: both the model evaluation (ROC over affinity maps) and the training data for the grouping readout rely on COCO annotation masks, which are known to be coarse and inconsistent. The 'novel' metric is also conceptually close to prior affinity-based analyses (LOST, TokenCut, dense ViT descriptors), so its novelty is limited.

The central comparison between architecture and training objective remains confounded despite the caveat: DINO models are trained on proprietary-scale data (LVD, web-scale), supervised baselines on ImageNet, and the Gram teacher (DINOv3) is itself the strongest model. Dataset scale, data distribution, and objective are not decoupled, and with only 9 models the across-model correlation (Spearman r=0.950 on n=9 points) is over-interpreted as evidence of a 'general principle'.

The Gram alignment result is somewhat expected by construction: distilling from DINOv3, the model that already performs best on the evaluation metric, and then showing improved alignment with that metric risks confirmation rather than independent evidence. The claim that this 'converges with' DINOv3's Gram anchoring is suggestive but the causal story is weaker than presented.

Only last-layer features are used for the behavior-prediction experiments, while layer-wise analyses are shown only for DINOv3 object-centricity; a fuller layer sweep across models would strengthen (or qualify) the conclusions. The manuscript is also thin in the main text, with key results (raw correlations, condition-split analyses, CLS baseline) relegated entirely to the supplement.
No discussion of limitations regarding stimulus selection, demographic narrowness of the sample, or generalization beyond COCO; no societal-impact discussion.

strengths: The paper introduces a valuable, well-controlled behavioral benchmark (two-dot same/different judgments on naturalistic COCO scenes, ~1020 trials across 72 subjects with eye-tracking and careful counterbalancing) that meaningfully scales up classical psychophysics paradigms for object grouping, addressing a genuine gap noted in the field (e.g., prior work used only ~24 hand-picked images).

The experimental methodology is rigorous: matched distances across same/different conditions to rule out distance-based shortcuts, eye-tracking with fixation-break exclusion, noise-ceiling normalization of model-human Spearman correlations, nested cross-validation for RT prediction, and a linear-readout baseline confirming results are not an artifact of MLP capacity.

The proposed object-centric metric (ROC analysis over patch affinity maps against ground-truth object boundaries) is simple, interpretable, and supervision-free with respect to model training, and the finding that object-centric AUC strongly predicts behavioral alignment across architectures and training objectives (Spearman r=0.95) is a clean, unifying empirical result.

The Gram-alignment experiments are the most interesting part: fine-tuning supervised models to distill Gram matrix structure from DINOv3 improves grouping accuracy, object-centricity, and behavioral alignment without changing ImageNet accuracy, and the CLS-token distillation control in the supplement convincingly isolates patch-level correlation structure as the active ingredient. This converges with DINOv3's Gram-anchoring design and provides actionable insight for model design.
The paper is clearly written, with honest hedging (e.g., acknowledging architecture and training objective are not fully decoupled), and code/data availability supports reproducibility.
The behavioral results themselves (same-object advantage, its interaction with dot distance, isotropy across directions) replicate and extend known effects, validating the benchmark's utility.
weaknesses: Confounds between training regime and data scale are only partially addressed: DINO models are trained on far larger datasets than supervised counterparts (the 'Large dataset' column in Table 1 makes this explicit), so the headline claim that 'training objective rather than architecture drives object-centricity' could partly reflect data scale. The Gram-alignment result mitigates this but does not fully resolve it.

The central correlation (object-centric AUC vs. behavioral alignment, r=0.95) is computed across only 9 models, giving wide uncertainty on the Spearman estimate; no confidence intervals or significance assessment appropriate for n=9 are provided, and the reported p=0.0001 appears overstated. The causal interpretation (object-centricity 'drives' alignment) rests on a small number of points.

The behavioral dataset is modest in size for the RT-prediction task (255 images × 4 conditions); a noise ceiling of only 0.42 and raw model-human correlations capped at ~0.35 indicate the best models explain a limited fraction of trial-level variance, and conclusions about 'human-like' alignment should be tempered accordingly. The abstract's framing of 'strongest performance' is fair, but the gap to the noise ceiling deserves more emphasis.

The RT readout uses only two patch features (central and peripheral dot locations) concatenated into an MLP. This is a deliberately simple probe, but it discards most of the representation's spatial structure; alternative readouts (e.g., full affinity-map statistics between the two locations) might yield different model rankings and would strengthen the claim that the metric, not incidental feature details, drives alignment.

Potential circularity: the object-centricity metric is computed against the same COCO annotations used to construct and validate the behavioral stimuli, so both the metric and human behavior are anchored to COCO segmentation ground truth; the extent to which results depend on annotation quality is not analyzed.

The Gram-alignment experiment fine-tunes only the last block and distills from a much stronger teacher; even with the CLS control, it remains conceivable that some benefit comes from generic feature compression/regularization of a weak student by a powerful teacher rather than from Gram structure per se. Additional controls (e.g., distilling from a non-DINO strong teacher, or Gram distillation between two supervised models) would bolster the mechanistic claim.

Several important experimental details are deferred to supplementary material that reviewers and readers would benefit from in the main text (raw correlations, per-condition breakdowns), and some claims (e.g., 'steady improvement across model generations') rest on a limited model zoo lacking model-size scaling within a family.

Minor: the abstract's 'Code and data are available here' has no actual link (likely anonymization placeholder, but should be verified), and the claim of a 'novel' object-centric metric is somewhat overstated given prior work on affinity/attention-based segmentation quality measures (LOST, TokenCut, dense descriptor analyses).
